title: Management of Sclerotinia Stem Rot of Indian Mustard (Brassica juncia)
authors: Gaurav, Ramesh Singh and Anand Kumar Prajapati
affiliations: 1 Department of Plant Pathology T.D.P.G. College Jaunpur 222002

blocks.x: Introduction

Indian mustard (Brassica juncia) commonly known as rai or laha and belong to the family brassicaceae. The mediterranean region is considered the center of origin of this crop oilseed brassicas including rapeseed and mustard are the third most important source of vegetable edible oil in the world. Rapeseed-mustard crop is cultivated in about 53 countries and 6 continents, covering a large area globally. In India major mustard growing state include Rajasthan, M.P. Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, West bangal and Gujrat. Indian mustard can be grown successfully under both irrigated and rainfed condition, making it an important oilseed crop in different Agro-climatic region. Indian rapeseed-mustard have occupied production area 63.40 lakh hac. with an average yield of 1233.40-kilogram g/ha and the total production of 78.20 lakh tones. India is contributing to world in area 28.3 lakh hac. and production 19.8%. More than 20 diseases affect the crop with high economic bearings. Among the diseases stem rot caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Lib) de bary is next only to a Alternaria blight in importance. The disease Stem rot caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum was considered to be the disease of minor importance of rapeseed and mustard but due to newer agriculture technology and extensive cultivation of new varieties of crop susceptible to this fungus. It has assumed the greater importance in recent past. of late, it has assumed serious proportion and causing considerable damage to the crop in rapeseed and mustard growing area of Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.
Historical background of pathogen

The disease was first reported from Sweden in 1880 by Eriksson with the name of stem rot of clover caused by Sclerotinia trifoliorum Eriksson. Smith of North (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) on the basis of sclerotial size which ranged between 3-10.0 mm.

Smith (1900) concluded that this was a degenerative form of Sclerotinia libertiana. Jagger (1920) reported a similar small sclerotial type of Sclerotinia which was able to produce apothecia In-Vitro and described a new species, (Sclerotinia minor) to cause decay of lettuce, celery and other crops. Additional species of Sclerotinia subsequently mentioned below: described by different workers are mentioned below.
Sclerotinia intermedia Ramsey 1924 on salify and carrot. Sclerotinia trifoliorum Eriksson var. Fabae Keay (1939) on Vicia faba. Sclerotinia sativa Drayton and Groves (1943) on Tulipa and Melilotus.
Geographical Distribution

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum arise in fairly cool and humid area of the world. As the generalized report made by multiple individuals. However, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum also arise in localities usually deliberate to be hot and arid. When the temperature near the freezing temperature (00C) or when temperature more than 320C prevails, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum is much lower active than at level between these universal Excessive. The precise locality and the environmental situation prevalent at the time the disease or fungus observed were not specified S. sclerotiorum has been recorded from several countries located in all continents. It is possible that the fungus arises somewhere in almost every country.

Stem rot of rapeseed and mustard is wide spread and worldwide in occurrence and has been reported from other countries like Canada (Platford and Breiner, 1975; Morall, 1976; Dueck, 1977), Denmark (Anonymous, 1974), Germany (Kirchner and Pluschkel, 1979), United Kingdom (Rawlinson and Muthgalu, 1979), and Nepal (Chaudhary, 1993).

In India, Shaw and Ajrekar (1915) reported this disease for the first time from Pusa, Bihar. Since then, it was found to occur in other parts of the 13 countries. Mehta et al. (1946) reported stem rot disease on Eruca sativa. Recently, stem rot of rapeseed and mustard emerged in serious form in many parts of the country Viz., Haryana, Himanchal Pradesh, Punjab, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam, Andman-Nikobar and Rajasthan (Roy, 1973; Lodha et al., 1992; Kumar and Thakur, 2000; Shivpuri et al., 2000; Chattopadhyay et al., 2002, 2004; Prasad and Kumar, 2007. Chauhan et al. (1992) reported that stem rot of mustard caused yield losses up to 72 per cent in severe cases in Uttar Pradesh. Six hundred and forty fields were surveyed in 24 districts of Rajasthan by Ghasolia et al. (2004) and 40-60% disease incidence was recorded in 31 fields of 10 districts and 20- 39% disease incidence of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum in 71 fields and in rest of the 538 fields were found less than 20 per cent disease incidence.
Symptomatology

The pathogen Sclerotinia sclerotiorum attack all the portion of mustard plant and developed different kind of symptoms in serious condition. Sclerotia of the fungus may be produced on the outer surface of the root where they are entirely apparent and causing root rot. The stalk of the mustard plants displayed the symptoms of the soon, as the stalk is the primary aim of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. On the stem, the disease shows up as lengthened water-soaked area (Fig.-1).

Fig.-1: On the stem, the disease shows up as lengthened water-soaked area. Thereafter on this water-soaked areas are cover with cottony mycelial growth of the fungus. The lesions step by step rise in size and in suitable situation girdle the stem entirely resultant in wilting and demise of the plants. In several cases, the infection usually not spread much and get restricted to the lower area of the pith and thus resulted in stunting and premature maturation rather than sudden collapse and demise of plants. The afflicted region becomes white and trends shred and many grayish-white to black sclerotia of various forms and sizes appears on the surface of the lesions and also inside the stem pith (Fig.-2).
Fig.-2: Grayish-white to black sclerotia of various forms and sizes appears on the surface of the lesions and also inside the stem pith.

The water-soaked lesions are also repeatedly seen on leaves portion, which later on are covered with white mycelial growth of the pathogen. The injury was first showed up at the margin of leaves as faded green patches which soon turned to cottony and enlarging quickly down word and in ward in suitable weather situation. Ultimately, entire leaves were covered with white mycelial growth on the surface of the injury in four to six days (Fig.-3).

Fig.-3: Entire leaves were covered with white mycelial growth on the surface of the injury. The development of mycelium was also noticed to Disseminate on petioles and stalk causing premature defoliation of leaves and demise of plant. Cottony to black sclerotia were also observed on the surface of the injury (Fig.-4).
Fig.-4: Cottony to black sclerotia were also observed on the surface of the injury. Related symptoms were also notice on siliquae of infected plants (Fig.-5).
Fig.-5: symptoms were also notice on siliqua of infected plants.
As a result, few are sometimes no seed formation take place. White color mycelial growth of the pathogen near soil level has observed on the stem (Fig.-6).
Fig.-6: White colour mycelial growth of the pathogen near soil level has observed on the stem. In severe condition of this pathogen affected plant and field are completely destroyed (Fig.-7).

Fig-7: In severe condition of this pathogen affected plant and field are completely destroy. Pathogen has very wide host range and is known to infect about 400 plant spp. (Kolte, 1985) with no proven success of resistance. Morris and Swingle (1921) reported Sclerotinia rot in Sunflower as development of scaly lesions at soil level and rotting of root and crown. Verma and Verma (1993) in Safflower, observed symptoms of wilt, brown discoloration and rotting at the base of the capsule. Mycelial growth and dark sclerotia were observed inside the infected plants.

The symptoms of disease on Ajowan infected with Sclerotinia sclerotiorum appeared as wilting. Entire root system showed extensive rotting and infection resulting in death and decay of plants. Pathogen produced numerous sclerotia of different sizes in the pith region of dead plants. Infection also occurred on the stem at the soil level and on the foliage at their basses or on the foliage that came in contact with soil (Sattar and Alam, 1993). The symptoms of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum infection on other plant species like Cauliflower, French bean, Fennel, Parthenium and Neem have also reported by several workers (Shyam et al., 1994; Yanar et al., 1996; Ram Palat, 2001; Singh and Singh, 2004; Ghasolia and Shivpuri, 2004 a,b).
Taxonomy and Nomenclature

Peziza sclerotiorum of (Libert, 1937) was transferred by Fuckel to his new genus, Sclerotinia and the specific epithet was changed by him to libertiana resulting in the combination of Sclerotinia libertiana (Fuckel, 1970). However, it is preferred to use the original specific epithet in the combination of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum Fuckel (De-Bary, 1984).

The genus Sclerotinia was lectotypified 1928 by Honey, with Fuckle (1970). Whetzel (1945) transferred Sclerotinia candolleana to a new genus Ciborinia and ignoring Honey's lectotypification cited Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Lib.) de- Bary as the type species of Sclerotinia.

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, the typical representative of the family Sclerotiniaaceae, has been a source of controversy for many years. Its wide polyphagy attests adaptation possibilities and an unanimously accepted variability. It is supposed to be collective species made up of numberless physiological races (Crisan, 1977) in the rage of which Whetzel (1945) incudes other species of Sclerotinia also. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum is the typical representative of the family Sclerotiniaceae of sub-division Ascomycotina (Ainsworth, 1973).

The taxonomic position of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Lib.) de Bary, S. trifoliorum and S. minor Jagger has not yet been resolved. Many authors (Jagger, 1920; Keay, 1939; Whetzel, 1945; Bjorling, 1951; Williams and Western, 1965) considered them completely different, while others (Purdy, 1955; Walker, 1969; Morrall, 1976) recognized only one species i.e. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum.
Morphology of the pathogen

Morphological and cultural nature of the pathogen studied on PDA medium (in culture) and host (in nature for the identified of pathogen revealed that the communities in culture were cottony, compact, circular, fast growth and manufactured numerous sclerotia (Fig.-8).
Fig.-8: The pathogen growth on PDA media formed cottony, compact, circular, fast growth and manufactured numerous sclerotia.
Mycelium septate, branched, hyaline to light brown in colored and calculated in 10 to 19 mm in size (Fig.-9).
Fig.-9: Mycelium septet, branched, hyaline to light brown in colored.

Sclerotia-superficial, manufactured in 1 or 2 concentric rings on PDA medium within 15 days. Sclerotia are grayish white to black in colored, spherical to cylindrical or irregular in shape, measure 6.4-4.8 mm in size with soft to coarse and wrinkled surface (Fig.-10).

Fig.-10: Sclerotia are grayish white to black in colored, spherical to cylindrical or irregular in shape. On germination the sclerotia by germination of sclerotia to form apothecia (Fig.-11) and formed stalked apothecia, which were disc shaped and yellowish brown in colored and 3-6 mm in diameter (Fig.-12).
Fig.-11: On germination the sclerotia by germ tube

Fig.-12: Stalked apothecia, which were disc shaped and yellowish brown in colored. The Asci are inoperculate, cylindrical, narrow, rounded at the apex, 8 ascospores present in each asci and measuring 117-107 x 5.6-11 mm in size. Ascospores- hyaline, ellipsoidal, smooth wall, uniform in size and measuring 9.5-12.5 x 6.1-7.9 mm in size (Figure 19.10). The morphological characters of the fungus above agree very closely with those described by Kosasih and Willet (1975), Willet and Wong (1980) and Kolte (1985) for Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Lib.) de Bary and thus, the fungus was identified as such.
Host range

Sclerotinia is a cosmopolitan species with a broad host range of over 350 species of 60 family (Schwartz, 1974). 24 plant species as the hosts of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (twenty-eight) and some of them were Brassica spp., Capsicum spp. Sesame, Coriander, Chickpea, Sunflower and Tobacco plants. Roy, (1973) studies the host range of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and listed twenty-seven host of which were new record in India (Roy 1973). The number of plants species were recorded as the host of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum from time-to-time workers (Morrall 1976; Purdy,1979 Bilgrami et al 1979; Cristea et al., 1985; Shin and Lee, 1987; Rathore et al., 1993; Sattar et al., 1995; Ghasolia et al., 2004).
Epidemiology

Species of the Sclerotinia sclerotinia can role either as soil-borne or air-borne fungus. Infection of overground plant parts resulted from ascospore inoculum, whereas soil line infection may be resulted either from ascospore or sclerotia; underground infection, however resulted from mycelial sprouting of soil-borne sclerotia. Accordingly, the epidemiology of 2 type of infections incited by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum., is fairly different and the impact of weather factors on their incidence and development differs considerably.

The infection of beans occurs on aboveground parts and it seems unlikely that the large sclerotia of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum are an important form of inoculum and they function essentially to produce airborne ascospores (Abawi and Grogan, 1975; Cooke et al., 1975; Saiio, 1977; Schwartz and Steadman, 1978). Apothecia formation was observed at mean temperature of 9-17°C for 14 days periods. Number of apothecia and level of aerial infection, were not related to the amount of total monthly rainfall (Letham et al., 1967). The outbreak of white blight of mustard caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum of all the above ground parts of the plants was in cool and wet environment. A temperature of 20-25°C and relative humidity of 90-10 per cent was congenial for stalk rot (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) development in cauliflower (Sharma and Sharma, 1985). Low temperature and high moisture favored the development of sclerotia of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum on the surface of the pea under natural conditions (Sharma, 1985). Apothecia production in case of Sclerotinia spp. was governed by temperature between 0-30°C followed by intermediate R. H. 98 per cent (Achbani et al., 1995).
Integrated Disease management
Seed treatments

Seed treatment is considered one of most effective and economical method for managing plant disease. The combination of T. viride +Carbendazim and T. viride + Garlic extract showed the best result by reducing disease incidence up to 90.09 % followed by Companion + T. viride which reduced the disease incidence by 81.83% Seed coating either alone with fungicides or in combination with bio- agent significantly managed stem rot. Seed coating with Benomyl and Carbendazim has been recorded most effective against S. sclerotiorum in mustard (Singh et al., 1994). Seed treatment with garlic bulb extract, Trichoderma viride, Mancozeb and Carbendazim was found effective in reducing disease incidence and better plant stand in mustard crop (Chattopadhyay et al., 2002 and 2004).
Source of Resistance

Resistant varieties are the simplest, practical, effective and economical method of plant disease management. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum has an extremely wide host-range and has been reported to affect more than 408 species of plants. The dearth of reports before 1968 indicates that many researchers formally accepted the ideas that resistance to S. sclerotiorum did not exists (Steadman, 1979). Brun et al.,(1979). Studied the reaction of 150 rapeseed genotypes against. S. sclerotiorum. Rapeseed genotypes of Japanese origin showed some resistance to S. Sclerotiorum. Sharma and Sharma (1986) screened eight genotypes of Brassica oleracea against S. Sclerotiorum, and found that "Orena" and "Avans" were more tolerant to the pathogen. Singh et al., (1994) also, screened 12 Brassica spp. under natural and artificial conditions. They found Brassica napus and B. juncea cv. Rugosa posse's resistance in the field as well as under greenhouse conditions. The genotypes PCR 10, RW 8410, RW 9401 and RGH 8006 were observed resistant against stem rot (Pathak and Godika, 2002).
Effect of date of sowings

The choice of date of sowing in related to plant disease has one principle aims Viz. to decreased to a lowest the period over which infective agent (propagules, vectors) meets susceptible host tissue. Since most crops grown below range of temperature and humidity, wider than those favoring fungus growth, sowing or planting at season which gave the crop and advantage is obviously strategy. Incidence of the disease in infested S. sclerotiorum field, was lowest in early sown crop (Singh et al., 1979; Singh and Singh, 1984). The various sowing dates on the incidence of stem rot Pea caused by S. sclerotiorum, early sown (21 October) crop resulted in the greatest, whereas sowing in the end week of November, resulted in lowest disease incidence (Singh, 1996). The adjustment of date of sowing on the incidence of stem rot of Ajowan (Singh et al., 2002) and of Rajmash (Palat 2001) and Sclerotina blight of Brinjal (Singh, 2003) caused by S. sclerotiorum was recorded minimum disease incidence in In-Vivo condition.
Organic Amendments

Soil amendments is the most effective methods of bio control. The disease may be minimized by certain amendments due to suppressiveness. Stem rot disease caused by S. sclerotiorum was critical problem in cauliflower and the application of farm yard manure at 10-40 tones/acre gave efficacious control and decreases the number of sclerotia (Sandhu, 1992).
The Sclerotina soft rot of lettuce and survival rate of sclerotia of S. sclerotiorum were reduced by addition of organic amendments in field (Asirif et al., 1994).
The stalk rot of cauliflower caused by S. sclerotiorum in field condition reduced the disease intensity by the application of different soil amendment Aujala et al. 2001

The application of different soil amendments against S. sclerotiorum on Ajwain (Singh et al., 2000), Rajmash (Palat, 2001) brinjal (Singh et al., 2005a) were reduced the disease incidence in field conditions.
Cultural Management

Clean and heathy seed should be selected for the sowing. Deep ploughing the land during summer period and crop rotation with resistance host are essential for preventing the sclerotial population in the soil. Soil solarization through covered of transparent polythene (0.1mm) for 45 days has been observed an excellent management practice. Sharma et al., (2001) reported that the irrigation at pre sowing and supplemented with 3 irrigations at branching, flowering and at pod formation and decreases the disease incidence. Crop rotation with non-host crop helpful in reducing the disease incidence.
Effect of Plant extract

Singh et al., (2013) evaluated leaf extracts of seven plant species by Poison Food technique against Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Maximum inhibition 76% over control due to use of Makoy leaf extracts followed by Garlic, Sadabahar. Tulsi and Madar leaf extracts. Dahtura and Eucalyptus was lest effective against the test pathogen.

Bhandari and Mukherjee (1959) observed that bark obtained from the trunk of Neem contained number of chemical compound e.g. Nimbin (0.04%), Nibinin (0.001%), Nimbidin (0.4%), Nimbosteral (0.3), essential oil (0.02%) and Tannin (6.0%) and also recorded that neem oil yielded various acids sulphur.

Azadirachta indica commonly known as neem or morgosa is found throughout India. It has reputed value for medicinal (Chapra et al., 1952) and antifungal (Murthy and Sirsi, 1957). Recently Neem leaf powder has been successfully used for controlling a nematode disease incited by Meloidogyne spp. (Mukherjee and Tiagi, 1978).

Although, a preliminary report indicates that garlic bulb extract inhibits growth of same fungi but whether activity is identical to that of extracts from leaf (Mishra and Dixit, 1976; Singh et al., 1979) is still not clearly known.
Recently, garlic extract is shown to have fungicidal and inhibitory action against several fungal species including some that cause mycoses (Moore and Atkins, 1977).

The growing realization that plant extracts can be successfully exploited in agriculture has recently gained attention of several workers (Agrawal, 1978; Singh et al., 1979 and 1980) and control of plant pathogens by their use is becoming increasingly important as chemical methods based on fungicides are being replaced because of their limitations in causing health hazards. The effect of an aqueous leaf extract of garlic on the two pathogens Viz., Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. ciceri of Cicer arietinum studied by Singh et al. (1979) and found that the growth of the pathogens reduced greatly at 7000 and 5000 ppm, respectively. Seeds treated with garlic extract before sowing produced wilt free seedling.
Effect of Antagonist

Antagonism is the balance wheel of nature, where there is antagonism. In biological control, one exploits the natural enemies of the fungus to one’s benefit. Sharma et al. (1982) detect the 8 fungal antagonistic spp. antagonistic to S. sclerotiorum from rotted sclerotia and infected soil. Isolates of the T. viride, T. harzianum and Gliocladium roseum were topmost effective in inhibit the mycelial growth. Culture filtrate of these 3 antagonist was also effective in inhibition germination of sclerotia.
Singh and Singh 1998 studies the effect of T. Viride and

T. hargzianum culture filtrate on the growth of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum lab candition and field condition. They have also recorded that T. viride was superior than T. harzianum in checking for the disease management.
Chemical control

The endeavours made by many workers to evaluate effect of plant extract, bio- pesticides and chemical in inhibit the growth of S. sclerotiorum In-Vitro condition gave premising results. The Nimbidine gave about 94% growth inhibition over control (Singh et al., 2005b; Singh et al., 2003b). The fungicides namely Bavistin, Vitavax, Vapam and Topsin-M completely inhibit the growth of the fungus In-Vitro (Singh et al., 2003b; Palat et al., 2004; Roy and Saikia, 1976; Abdou et al., 1982; Singh and Gangopadhay, 1984). Germination of sclerotia was prevented by Vitavax, Benomyl and Thiram at 5ppm and caused about 60 per cent inhibition of mycelial growth of S. sclerotiorum, Captan and Thiram completely inhibited ascospore germination at 3-4 ppm. Benomyl at 1000 ppm reduced the viability of sclerotia (Howthorne and Jarvis, 1973). The effect of an aqueous leaf extract of garlic on S. sclerotiorum was studied and it was found that the growth of the pathogen reduced greatly (Singh et al., 1979). The garlic extract has fungicidal and inhibitory action against fungal spore (Moore and Atkins, 1977). Antifungal properties of neem product have also been noticsrtyared (Murty and Sirsi, 1957).
